nameStory: Selwyn's Pylaisia is named after Alfred Selwyn, a 19th-century British geologist who explored Canada and made significant contributions to North American natural history. The genus name Pylaisia honors Bory de Saint-Vincent's colleague Pylaie, a French botanist who studied mosses and algae in the early 1800s.
description: Selwyn's Pylaisia is a delicate, creeping moss that forms thin, silky mats on tree bark and occasionally rocks. This tiny moss creates feathery, flattened sprays that shimmer with a golden-green luster when dry and turn bright green when moist. The individual plants are quite small, typically growing only 1-2 centimeters tall, but they can spread to form patches several inches across.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thin, silky mats that feel smooth and feathery to the touch, with branches that lie flat against the substrate in elegant, pinnate patterns

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, overlapping leaves are lance-shaped and pressed close to the stem, giving the moss a flattened, almost scale-like appearance under a hand lens

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Displays a distinctive golden-green to yellowish sheen when dry that transforms to bright emerald green when wet

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on smooth bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring the trunk bases and lower branches of maples, birches, and oaks

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels remarkably silky and smooth when stroked gently with a finger, lacking the coarse or springy texture of many other bark mosses

habitat: Selwyn's Pylaisia is found growing on the bark of deciduous trees in mature forests throughout New England, though it's quite uncommon. It prefers smooth-barked trees like maples, birches, and young oaks, typically growing on the lower trunk and base of trees in moist, shaded woodland environments. Look for it in rich, mature forests with good canopy cover that maintain consistent humidity.

seasonality.spring: The moss becomes vibrant green as spring moisture returns, making it easier to spot against tree bark. This is an excellent time to observe its silky texture as it responds to increased humidity.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the moss takes on its characteristic golden-green sheen and becomes less noticeable. Sporophytes, when present, are most likely to be found during this season.
seasonality.fall: Autumn rains revive the bright green coloration, and the moss may be more visible as leaves fall and expose tree trunks. The contrast against colorful fallen leaves can help with spotting.
seasonality.winter: The moss remains visible year-round but appears somewhat dormant, often with a yellowish tinge. Snow and ice can make it harder to locate, but mild winter days offer good viewing opportunities.

funFact: This moss is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in the entire region, making anyone who finds it a genuine botanical detective who's spotted one of the region's most elusive plants!
confusionNotes: Selwyn's Pylaisia can be confused with its much more common relative, Many-flowered Leskea, but Selwyn's Pylaisia has a more distinctly silky, golden sheen when dry and forms thinner, more delicate mats. Remember: Selwyn's is silky and sparse, while Many-flowered Leskea is more robust and common.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called Pylaisia selwynii, this moss is sometimes still referred to by its old scientific name in older field guides. The extreme rarity of this species in New England means that any sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanists or natural heritage programs, as it could represent an important range extension or rare population.
compareHints: Compared to Many-flowered Leskea (the other Pylaisia in our region), Selwyn's Pylaisia forms much thinner, more delicate mats with a more pronounced silky texture and golden sheen when dry. Many-flowered Leskea tends to be more robust, forms thicker cushions, and lacks the distinctive golden luster that makes Selwyn's Pylaisia shimmer in the right light.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Many-flowered Leskea differs from its close relative Pylaisia selwynii primarily in leaf shape and sporophyte abundance—selwynii has more elongated leaves and produces fewer capsules.
